excerpt: Ratio, proportion and the unitary method trip up more Class 6 students than any other chapter in the first term. Here is the NCERT chapter in plain language, with two worked real-life case studies and a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Ask a Class 6 student to share 20 sweets between two children ‘in the ratio 3 to 2’ and watch what happens. Half will split it 3 and 2, hand back 15 sweets, and look puzzled. That single mix-up — treating a ratio as the actual amounts rather than the number of shares — is at the heart of the Class 6 maths ratio and proportion chapter, and it is why the topic deserves more care than it usually gets. Get the idea of a ratio right, and equivalent ratios, proportion and the unitary method all fall into line.

This is the NCERT Class 6 chapter, explained the way I explain it to eleven-year-olds: one idea at a time, with numbers you can picture. At the end there are two solved case studies and a short quiz.

What a ratio really means

A ratio compares two quantities of the same kind by division. If a class has 18 girls and 12 boys, the ratio of girls to boys is 18 : 12. The colon is read ‘to’. Order matters — 18 : 12 is girls to boys, and 12 : 18 is boys to girls, and those are not the same statement.

Two things students forget. First, both quantities must be in the same unit before you compare. To compare 2 metres with 50 centimetres, convert first: 200 cm : 50 cm, which is 4 : 1. Second, a ratio has no unit of its own — it is just a comparison, a pure number relationship.

Equivalent ratios and simplifying

Go back to the sweets. 20 shared in the ratio 3 : 2 means 3 + 2 = 5 equal shares, so each share is 20 ÷ 5 = 4 sweets. One child gets 3 × 4 = 12, the other 2 × 4 = 8. Notice 12 : 8 is the same ratio as 3 : 2 — multiply both parts of 3 : 2 by 4 and you land on 12 : 8. Ratios that describe the same comparison are equivalent ratios.

You make equivalent ratios by multiplying or dividing both parts by the same number. To write a ratio in its simplest form, divide both parts by their highest common factor. For 18 : 12, the HCF is 6, so 18 : 12 = 3 : 2. Always leave your final answer in simplest form unless the question asks otherwise — it is the mathematical equivalent of tidying up after yourself.

Proportion and the cross-product check

When two ratios are equal, the four numbers are said to be in proportion. We write 3 : 4 :: 6 : 8, read as ‘3 is to 4 as 6 is to 8’. The outer numbers (3 and 8) are the extremes; the inner numbers (4 and 6) are the means.

Here is the check worth memorising: four numbers are in proportion when the product of the extremes equals the product of the means. For 3 : 4 :: 6 : 8, extremes give 3 × 8 = 24 and means give 4 × 6 = 24. They match, so yes, these are in proportion. This cross-product test is faster and safer than simplifying both ratios and hoping they look alike.

Quick example: are 2 : 5 and 6 : 15 in proportion? Cross-multiply: 2 × 15 = 30 and 5 × 6 = 30. Equal, so they are in proportion.

The unitary method

The unitary method is the chapter’s most useful tool for life outside the exam hall. The idea: first find the value of one unit, then multiply up to however many you need.

  • Step 1 — find one. If 6 notebooks cost ₹90, one notebook costs 90 ÷ 6 = ₹15.
  • Step 2 — scale up. Then 10 notebooks cost 15 × 10 = ₹150.

Divide to get down to one, multiply to get up to many. That is the whole method. It quietly powers unit rates, speed, currency conversion and recipe scaling for years to come, which is exactly why NCERT plants it here in Class 6.

Case study 1: scaling a recipe

A kheer recipe for 4 people uses 2 cups of rice and 6 cups of milk. Meera is cooking for 10 people. How much of each does she need?

Use the unitary method. For 4 people: 2 cups rice, so for 1 person that is 2 ÷ 4 = 0.5 cup; for 10 people, 0.5 × 10 = 5 cups of rice. Milk: 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5 cups per person, then 1.5 × 10 = 15 cups of milk. Notice the ratio of rice to milk stays 2 : 6 = 1 : 3 throughout — scaling a recipe is really just holding a ratio steady while both parts grow.

Case study 2: a map and a shopping bill

On a map, 1 cm represents 5 km. Two towns are 7 cm apart on the map. Real distance? By the unitary method, 1 cm is 5 km, so 7 cm is 5 × 7 = 35 km.

Now a shopping check with proportion. If 3 kg of apples cost ₹240, do 5 kg at ₹400 keep the same rate? Set up 3 : 240 and 5 : 400 and cross-multiply: 3 × 400 = 1200 and 240 × 5 = 1200. Equal, so the price per kilo is consistent — the shopkeeper is charging fairly. This is the kind of everyday reasoning the case-study questions are built to train.

The eight-question quiz below covers exactly what we walked through — simplifying ratios, spotting equivalent ratios, the cross-product proportion check and the unitary method. quiz.title: Class 6 Ratio and Proportion Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on simplifying ratios, equivalent ratios, proportion and the unitary method. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: Simplify the ratio 18 : 12 to its lowest terms.
questions.explanation: Divide both parts by the HCF, which is 6: 18 ÷ 6 = 3 and 12 ÷ 6 = 2, giving 3 : 2.
Multiply both parts of 2 : 3 by 4 to get 8 : 12, so 8 : 12 is equivalent to 2 : 3.

questions.q: The ratio of 2 metres to 50 cm is:
questions.explanation: First make the units the same: 2 m = 200 cm, so 200 : 50 = 4 : 1.
Cross-multiply: 3 × 8 = 24 and 4 × 6 = 24. The products are equal, so they are in proportion.

questions.q: If 6 pens cost ₹90, what does 1 pen cost?
If 1 pen costs ₹15, what do 10 pens cost?
In the proportion 5 : 8 :: 15 : ?, what is the missing number?
questions.explanation: 5 : 8 becomes 15 : ? by multiplying both parts by 3, so the missing number is 8 × 3 = 24.

questions.q: 20 sweets are shared in the ratio 3 : 2. How many does the first child get?
questions.explanation: There are 3 + 2 = 5 shares, so one share is 20 ÷ 5 = 4. The first child gets 3 × 4 = 12.

faq.q: What is the difference between a ratio and a proportion?
faq.a: A ratio compares two quantities of the same kind, like 3 : 2. A proportion is a statement that two ratios are equal, like 3 : 2 :: 6 : 4. Put simply, a proportion is two ratios set equal to each other.

faq.q: Why must both quantities be in the same unit before writing a ratio?
faq.a: Because a ratio compares size directly. Comparing 2 m with 50 cm as 2 : 50 is wrong — convert first to 200 cm : 50 cm, which correctly simplifies to 4 : 1.

faq.q: How does the cross-product check for proportion work?
faq.a: Four numbers a : b :: c : d are in proportion when a × d equals b × c — the product of the extremes equals the product of the means. If the two products match, the ratios are equal.

faq.q: When should I use the unitary method?
faq.a: Whenever you know the value of a group and need the value of a different-sized group. Find the value of one unit first by dividing, then multiply up to the quantity you want.
